items.title: 45 degrees is only optimal for a projectile in a vacuum
items.claim: Every physics textbook says the maximum range for a projectile is at launch angle 45 degrees. True in vacuum. In real air, the optimum angle is significantly less — and for some launches it's barely above 30 degrees.
items.prompt: Why does air change the optimum?

options.text: It doesn't — 45 degrees is always optimal
Air resistance reduces both horizontal velocity and vertical velocity, but the loss to drag is greater on long airborne paths; lowering the angle reduces flight time and total drag exposure
Gravity is different at high angles

items.reveal:
Vacuum case: range = (v^2 / g) * sin(2 * theta). Maximised at theta = 45 degrees.

With linear drag (low-speed air): the optimum angle decreases with launch speed and drag coefficient. For a thrown baseball or shot put, optimum is ~42-43 degrees.

With quadratic drag (more realistic at high speed): for a golf ball, optimum is closer to 12-15 degrees (combined with backspin for lift). For an artillery shell, often 30-40 degrees due to high muzzle velocity and dense air.

Why: higher launch angles mean longer flight times, more time exposed to drag, more total energy lost. The trade-off between vertical reach and drag loss shifts the optimum downward.

For a long-jumper, who launches around 7-10 m/s, the optimum angle calculated from biomechanics is ~22 degrees, not 45 — because the long-jumper cannot achieve high vertical velocity from horizontal sprint and because air resistance is minor. Body-mechanics constraints matter more than the equation.

The 45° result is a useful first approximation but should not be taken as universal. Most real-world projectile design uses computational fluid dynamics rather than analytical formulas.
items.why: Textbook results assume ideal conditions. In real applications (golf, baseball, artillery, athletics), the answer is shifted — often substantially — by drag and biomechanical constraints. 'Theoretically 45°' is correct for nothing on Earth.

items.title: London to Tokyo flights cross Siberia — not because Russia is convenient
items.claim: On a flat map, the shortest path between London and Tokyo looks like a horizontal line through Central Asia. The ACTUAL shortest path on Earth's surface arcs north over Siberia. That's the great-circle route.
items.prompt: Why is the great-circle route shortest?

options.text: Any geodesic (shortest path) on a sphere is part of a great circle — a circle whose plane passes through the sphere's centre. Latitude lines (except the equator) are NOT great circles, so flying along a latitude isn't optimal

items.reveal:
A geodesic is the shortest path between two points on a surface. On a flat plane, geodesics are straight lines. On a sphere, geodesics are arcs of great circles — circles whose centre coincides with the sphere's centre.

All meridians (longitude lines, including the prime meridian and date line) are great circles. The equator is a great circle. Lines of latitude EXCEPT the equator are NOT great circles — they're small circles whose plane does not pass through Earth's centre.

London-Tokyo: separated by ~9600 km along the great-circle route, ~12000 km if you fly along the line of latitude (~50°N).

Map projections distort geodesics:
- Mercator projection (Gerardus Mercator, 1569): preserves angles (conformal), shows rhumb lines as straight, but distorts areas and great-circle paths.
- Gnomonic projection: shows great circles as straight lines, but is unsuitable as a navigational chart.
- Robinson, Mollweide: balance distortions in different ways.

Airlines plan routes along great circles, adjusted for winds (jetstream eastbound from US to Europe saves an hour). 'Polar' routes from North America to East Asia routinely cross the Arctic.

In general relativity, geodesics on curved spacetime trace the paths of free-falling objects — gravity IS geodesic motion through curved spacetime.
items.why: Maps lie about distances. Modern navigation requires understanding that the shortest path on a sphere is curved on a flat map. The intuition fails everywhere except locally.

items.title: Matrices don't commute — and that's why quantum mechanics works
items.claim: AB is not generally equal to BA for matrices. The order of operations matters. This isn't a defect — it's the most important feature of matrix algebra and the mathematical foundation of quantum uncertainty.

options.text: Matrices represent linear transformations of vectors; applying transformation A then B is generally not the same as B then A. The non-commutativity reflects that composition of transformations in higher dimensions does NOT commute in general
AB = BA always works for invertible matrices

items.reveal:
For matrices, AB and BA are generally different — and AB is well-defined only when A's columns equal B's rows. Even for square matrices of the same size, AB and BA can differ wildly.

Example: A = [[1, 1], [0, 1]], B = [[1, 0], [1, 1]].
AB = [[2, 1], [1, 1]].
BA = [[1, 1], [1, 2]]. Different.

When does AB = BA? Some special cases: scalar multiples of identity; same diagonal matrix; simultaneously diagonalisable matrices; powers of the same matrix.

The commutator [A, B] = AB - BA measures the non-commutativity. For ordinary numbers it's always zero; for matrices it can be anything.

In QUANTUM MECHANICS:
- Physical observables are represented as matrices (or operators on Hilbert space).
- The commutator of position and momentum: [x, p] = i * hbar. Non-zero!
- Heisenberg's uncertainty principle: the variance of two non-commuting observables, in any state, has a lower bound proportional to the commutator. You can't simultaneously know position and momentum precisely.

This is not a measurement limitation — it's a structural feature of the math. Eigenvectors of non-commuting matrices are different; states have to choose between definite x and definite p.

Lie groups and algebras: continuous symmetry transformations form groups whose generators are matrices with commutation relations. The group SU(3) underlies the strong nuclear force; SU(2) describes weak force and quantum spin; U(1) describes electromagnetism. The standard model of particle physics is built from non-commuting matrices.

In computer graphics: rotation matrices in 3D don't commute (mentioned in another card). The order matters when composing transformations.
items.why: Multiplication seems naturally commutative. For matrices it isn't — and the depth of this fact is that quantum mechanics, particle physics, computer graphics, and most of modern physics rely on it.
